blocks.text: We must now say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we have said, other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in the Nubian Geography, Clim. 1. section 1, translates it as white weasel. Golius gives hay weasel, commonly called fovina [beech marten] (because that most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alluded to foenum [hay], and that fovina [beech marten] was derived from foenum [hay], whereas it takes its name from the French word for beech). For Giggeius, فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain very useful animal, from whose skin fur garments are obtained. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [al-fanak ḥārr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farʾʾ yujlab kathīran] [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalī ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn lubs al-fanak] Phenec is an animal whose skin is warm, pleasantly scented, and the most fragrant of all kinds of fur. It is brought in great quantities from Secalia. Its flesh seems to be sweet. Its skin is colder than the skin of τοῦ [tou] simor, but warmer than the skin of τοῦ [tou] sungiab. It is customary to wear this skin especially in advancing age. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-l-qamāqim wa-l-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa] The skins of alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil, are moderately warm, and also light. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwaybba yūk hadh minhā al-farw qāla Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb] Alphenec, a small animal from which fur is obtained. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and that very large quantities are brought from the Slavic region. This is how the passage above should be read, not صقالية [ṣaqāliyya] Secalia (the Slavic region, that is, the region of the Slavs, was formerly in European Scythia, toward the western Ocean, as Simocatta attests in book 6, chapter 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-l-sinjāb wa-l-sammūr kull dhālika sabuʿ ka-l-thaʿlab wa-Ibn ʿirs] Phenec, and sungiab, and simur are all beasts of prey, like the fox and the weasel. Such are their statements, from which it would seem possible to infer that these furs belong among the kinds of martens. Nevertheless, الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec po[?]

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls Venetian and Agricola calls Finnish, after the Veneti and Finni, peoples on the Vistula in Prussia, by whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy says the following in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι· [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi] Along the river Vistula, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finni. It seems, I say, to be from these Finni that the Finnish mouse takes its name, and in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec; from its size and color the French call it petigris ^{(4)}. But سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab is also, according to Golius, a squirrel, an ash-colored animal, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium [vermilion] (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says that it is an animal shaped like a mole, larger than a mouse, living at the tops of trees, with a bluish skin, very soft and very beautiful, which people of luxurious tastes wear. It is apparent that a species of squirrel is being described. The simur is also a kind of mouse, not altogether unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais] [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας· [chrōntai pros chitōnas] Simor is the name given among the Parthians to a certain species of wild mouse, whose skins are used for clothing. According to others, the simur is a marten. Damir says that it is an animal resembling a cat, or, according to some, النمس [al-nims] a ferret, whose skin so excels in softness, lightness, warmth, and beauty that kings and great men wear it. I could add much more about both kinds of fur, drawn from the books of the Arabs; but to explain all these matters more precisely is beyond the leisure available to us, and contributes little to the present subject.
There is equal inconsistency among the Greeks in explaining the word שפן saphan.
1. Some render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous]; thus the Vulgate translator gives little hares, a rendering we have already examined above.

2. There were some who preferred hyena, such as Clement of Alexandria, in book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 10, where he represents Moses as saying, Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν, [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan] You shall not eat the hare or the hyena, that is, הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ, [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē] Nor shall you eat the hare. And a little later, Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ, [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē] for which the old translation has Nor shall you eat the beast. I would prefer beluum [hyena], or belbum [hyena]. For thus Julius Capitolinus, in his Gordian III: Under Gordian there were at Rome 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards [II, 418], 10 belbi [hyenas], that is, hyenas. Yet Philoxenus, in the Glossary, has Ὕαινα· ζῶον, [Hyaina; zōon] beast.
